title: OpenCV Reference
description: A quick reminder of the ideas and examples in the OpenCV lessons. Open the linked lesson when you need more help.

entries.name: An image is a number array
entries.summary: OpenCV is a library for working with images. A small colour image can be stored as rows, columns and three colour values per pixel.

example.code:
import cv2
import numpy as np

image = np.zeros((3, 4, 3), dtype=np.uint8)
print(image.shape)

notes: Array shape lists height before width; mixing them up swaps the intended picture size.

entries.name: Know the BGR channel order
entries.summary: OpenCV commonly uses blue, green, red order for colour images. Each uint8 channel can hold a whole number from 0 to 255.

example.code:
import cv2
import numpy as np

image = np.zeros((1, 1, 3), dtype=np.uint8)
image[0, 0] = [255, 0, 0]
print(image[0, 0].tolist())

notes: Many other image tools use RGB order; check the order before passing images between tools.

entries.name: Convert BGR to RGB
entries.summary: A colour conversion can reorder channels so another tool reads them correctly. COLOR_BGR2RGB swaps the blue and red positions.

example.code:
import cv2
import numpy as np

bgr = np.array([[[255, 0, 0]]], dtype=np.uint8)
rgb = cv2.cvtColor(bgr, cv2.COLOR_BGR2RGB)
print(rgb[0, 0].tolist())

notes: Reordering channels changes the representation; it does not mean the visible colour should change.

entries.name: Make a grayscale image
entries.summary: Grayscale stores one brightness value per pixel. It drops colour detail while keeping a brightness view useful for some image operations.

example.code:
import cv2
import numpy as np

bgr = np.full((2, 3, 3), 100, dtype=np.uint8)
gray = cv2.cvtColor(bgr, cv2.COLOR_BGR2GRAY)
print(gray.shape, gray[0, 0].item())

notes: Grayscale conversion is not simply taking the blue channel for every coloured pixel.

entries.name: Crop by rows and columns
entries.summary: Cropping selects a rectangle from an image. NumPy slices use start positions and stop just before the end positions.

example.code:
import cv2
import numpy as np

image = np.arange(20, dtype=np.uint8).reshape(4, 5)
crop = image[1:3, 2:5].copy()
print(crop.tolist())

notes: A slice can share memory with its source; use copy when you need independent pixels.

entries.name: Resize to a chosen size
entries.summary: Resizing changes image dimensions. OpenCV resize takes the target size as width, height, unlike the row-first array shape.

example.code:
import cv2
import numpy as np

image = np.zeros((4, 6, 3), dtype=np.uint8)
small = cv2.resize(image, (3, 2), interpolation=cv2.INTER_NEAREST)
print(small.shape)

notes: Changing width and height by different factors can stretch the picture.

entries.name: Threshold brightness
entries.summary: Thresholding turns brightness values into two groups. A binary threshold sets values above the limit to a maximum and the rest to zero.

example.code:
import cv2
import numpy as np

gray = np.array([[50, 100, 150]], dtype=np.uint8)
_, binary = cv2.threshold(gray, 100, 255, cv2.THRESH_BINARY)
print(binary.tolist())

notes: The exact comparison depends on the selected threshold mode.

entries.name: Blur nearby pixels
entries.summary: Blurring combines neighbouring pixel values to soften local changes. A kernel is the small neighbourhood used for the calculation.

example.code:
import cv2
import numpy as np

image = np.zeros((5, 5), dtype=np.uint8)
image[2, 2] = 255
blurred = cv2.GaussianBlur(image, (3, 3), 0)
print(int(blurred[2, 2]) < 255, int(blurred[2, 1]) > 0)

notes: A blur can hide useful detail as well as noise.

entries.name: Find candidate edges
entries.summary: An edge is a strong image change, often in brightness. Canny finds candidate edges after several processing steps; an edge is not an object label.

example.code:
import cv2
import numpy as np

image = np.zeros((20, 20), dtype=np.uint8)
image[5:15, 5:15] = 255
edges = cv2.Canny(image, 50, 150)
print(edges.shape, bool(np.any(edges)))

notes: Edge detection does not understand what an object is or whether it is safe.

entries.name: Draw with image coordinates
entries.summary: OpenCV drawing points use x, y order. x is the column and y is the row. A negative thickness can fill a shape.

example.code:
import cv2
import numpy as np

image = np.zeros((5, 5, 3), dtype=np.uint8)
cv2.rectangle(image, (1, 1), (3, 3), (0, 255, 0), thickness=-1)
print(image[2, 2].tolist(), image[0, 0].tolist())

notes: Array indexing is row, column, but drawing points are x, y.

entries.name: Use a mask to select pixels
entries.summary: A mask is an image that marks which pixels to include. In this operation, a nonzero mask value allows the source pixel through.

example.code:
import cv2
import numpy as np

image = np.array([[10, 20], [30, 40]], dtype=np.uint8)
mask = np.array([[255, 0], [0, 255]], dtype=np.uint8)
selected = cv2.bitwise_and(image, image, mask=mask)
print(selected.tolist())

notes: The mask needs matching image width and height and a suitable single-channel type.

entries.name: Save a small local picture
entries.summary: imwrite saves image pixels to a file. Check its return value and choose a practice path so you do not overwrite work you need.

example.code:
import cv2
import numpy as np

image = np.full((10, 10, 3), [0, 255, 0], dtype=np.uint8)
saved = cv2.imwrite("practice-green.png", image)
print(saved)

notes: A saved picture is not uploaded anywhere by this code; sharing is a separate action.
